Stage 4 · The language of impressions

Praise, reservation, verdict

Relative clauses do the describing, and a small set of fixed phrases does the judging. A review needs both.

Two habits separate a review from a reaction: name the thing precisely with a relative clause, and put every reservation next to the praise it qualifies.

4 · One opinion, six wordings.

the projection that filled the whole facade  →  which one.

1 · Read the explanation.
Saying what you thought, precisely

Name the thing first. A review that says the light show was amazing tells the reader nothing. Relative clauses do the naming: the projection that filled the whole facade, the square, which was packed by eight, the artist whose work was in the phone box. Defining clauses take no commas and say which one; non-defining clauses take commas and add a fact.

Emphasise with a cleft. What I particularly liked was the contrast of old and new is stronger than I liked the contrast, because the reader waits for the noun. The highlight for me was… does the same job. Use one or two in a review; more, and the trick shows.

Soften every reservation. English reviews put criticism next to praise and hedge it: a bit, not really, slightly, …, though, the only thing I am not so keen on is…, don’t get me wrong. Without the hedges the same content reads as an attack.

Blame the gap, not the object. It didn’t live up to my expectations and I didn’t really see the point of it both leave room for the reader to disagree, which a review should.

Finish with a verdict. A review that never says whether to go has not finished. It is worth going for the last ten minutes alone, I would go back, but on a weekday.

The commonest errors at this level
  • Adjectives with nothing under them: very nice, very interesting, four times.
  • Criticism with no hedge, which reads as anger rather than judgement.
  • That after a comma in a non-defining clause.
  • Live up with, packed of people, critical about somebody.
  • No verdict at the end, so the reader still does not know whether to go.

Two things to watch

1 — Every adjective needs a noun under it. Stunning is worth nothing on its own; stunning, especially the reds against the wet stone is a review.

2 — Hedges are not weakness. A bit, not really, for my liking tell the reader how far to trust the complaint, which is exactly what a reader wants to know.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Turning a reaction into a review sentence

The reaction: The light show was amazing but too crowded. Two words, no information.

Step 1 — name what was good, with a clause. Which part? the projection that filled the whole facade of the town hall.

Step 2 — emphasise it if it deserves emphasis. What I particularly liked was the projection that filled the whole facade.

Step 3 — attach the reservation next to it, hedged. …, although the square, which was packed by eight, made it hard to see twice.

Step 4 — add a verdict with a condition. It is worth going for that one projection alone, but on a weekday.

The result: three clauses, one hedge and a recommendation the reader can act on.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Putting the good bit last

A review needs emphasis, and English gets it by moving the important thing to the end of the sentence. That is what a cleft does: What I particularly liked was the contrast between the two halves. Compare the flat version — I particularly liked the contrast — and notice where your eye stops. The pattern is What + subject + verb + was / were + the thing, and the verb agrees with what follows: What impressed me were the crowds.

The highlight for me was… does the same job for a single best moment. Both are worth having: a review that reports without emphasising reads like a timetable.

Reservations, and why they are not attacks

English hedges criticism heavily, and the hedges are fixed: a bit…, not really…, …, though. I found it a bit loud, though carries two hedges, and the final though is a word you cannot move to the front in this use. I didn’t really see the point of it leaves the other person room to disagree, which is the point.

Three moves worth learning whole. Limiting a complaint: The only thing I am not so keen on is the queue — everything else is approved, and the complaint is fenced. Protecting the other speaker: Don’t get me wrong, I enjoyed it — said before the qualification, never after. Disappointment: It didn’t live up to my expectations — note that this describes the gap between the thing and your hopes, not the thing itself, which is why it is a fair way to be negative.

And a review has to end with a verdict: It is worth going for the ending alone. Worth takes an -ing form (worth to go), and alone after the noun means ‘even if there were nothing else’.

Errors to watch: What I liked was the crowds → were · It is worth to see → worth seeing · Though, I found it a bit loud at the start → put though at the end · I enjoyed it, don’t get me wrong as a qualification → it comes first.

Stage 5 · Speaking & WritingWriting

Writing a review

Four hundred people will read it and one of them will decide whether to spend a Saturday on your advice.

The brief

Review an event you actually attended: a festival, a concert, an exhibition, a match, a conference. Say what it was, name the best part precisely, give one honest reservation, and finish with a verdict a reader can act on. No adjective is allowed to stand without something under it.

Useful language

Partner AYou · reviewing

1 · Read the model review.
Model · a review in four paragraphs

The winter light festival runs for eleven nights across four streets and the old town square, and it is free. It began during an economic recession, when the council needed something that would fill hotels without filling a budget, and it has developed from one street into most of the centre.

What I particularly liked was the projection that covered the whole facade of the town hall: a field of flowers opening in time with the music, magnificent at a distance and slightly frightening from underneath. The colours in the river installation are stunning, and the final ten minutes, when everything runs at once, are genuinely thrilling.

The square, which was packed by eight, is the fault in the plan. Nothing has been done to protect older visitors from the crowd, and selling four thousand timed tickets for a space that size seems irresponsible rather than merely optimistic. The fish installation, praised in every listing I read, did not live up to my expectations either; I did not really see the point of it, though I may have been the wrong audience.

It is worth going for that one projection alone. Go on a weekday, arrive after nine, and start from the river end. The programme has enormous potential, and about half of it is currently spent on queuing.
